'''Haverstraw''' ({{IPA|en|ˈhæːvəɹstɹɔː|audio|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Noaius Paticus-Haverstraw.wav}}) is a [[Administrative divisions of New York#Village|village]] incorporated in 1854 in the [[Administrative divisions of New York#Town|town]] of [[Haverstraw, New York|Haverstraw]] in [[Rockland County, New York]], United States. It is located north of [[Congers, New York|Congers]], southeast of [[West Haverstraw, New York|West Haverstraw]], east of [[Garnerville, New York|Garnerville]], northeast of [[New City, New York|New City]], and west of the [[Hudson River]] at its widest point. As of the [[2020 United States Census|2020 census]], the population was 12,323.<ref name="Census 2020">{{Cite web |title=2020 Census Redistricting Data: Haverstraw village; New York|url=https://data.census.gov/table?q=Haverstraw+village;+New+York |access-date=June 9, 2023 |website=data.census.gov |publisher=U.S. Census Bureau}}</ref>

The village of Haverstraw is within the [[North Rockland Central School District]] public primary and secondary school system of [[New York State]], and the downtown hosts the [[Rockland Community College|Rockland Community College – Haverstraw Extension]] Center. {{As of|2009|url=http://www.voh-ny.com/mayor.htm}}, the mayor is Michael Kohut.<ref name="mayor">{{cite web|url=http://www.voh-ny.com/mayor.htm|title=The Village of Haverstraw Mayor's Message|access-date=November 5, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717230156/http://www.voh-ny.com/mayor.htm|archive-date=July 17, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==History==
===Settlement (1609–1750)===
[[File:Broadway Haverstraw.jpg|thumb|250px|left|Downtown Haverstraw]]
Before [[Netherlands|Dutch]] settlers traveled to the [[Hudson Valley|Hudson River Valley]] in the early part of the seventeenth century, the [[Rumachenanck tribe|Rumachenanck]] people, a subset of the [[Lenape]] tribe, called the area home. In 1609, during one of the many voyages the Dutch financed in search of the [[Northwest Passage]], [[Henry Hudson]] sailed the [[Hudson River]].

The village is one of the first to appear on maps of North America, listed as ''Haverstroo'', which means "oat straw" as an anglicized version of a Dutch word. The area was first referred to as Haverstroo in 1616. From 1686 till 1719, the present town of Haverstraw was included in the laws, taxes and militia duties of [[Orangetown]]. But that valley was increasing so rapidly in population, the distance was so great and the trail so poor between it and [[Tappan, New York|Tappan]], that the inhabitants petitioned for separate existence and on June 24, 1719, the following act was passed: "An Act to enable the Precincts of Haverstraw in the County of Orange, to chuse a Supervisor, a Collector, two Assessors, one Constable, and two Overseers of Highways."<ref name="ReferenceA">History of Rockland County by Reverend David Cole, 1884</ref>

The village was not incorporated as a municipality until March 11, 1854, as the Village of Warren, after [[Joseph Warren]], a major general who died at the [[Battle of Breed's Hill]] (a.k.a. [[Battle of Bunker Hill|Bunker Hill]]) in 1775 during the [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]].<ref name="town_history_page_5">{{cite web|url=http://www.townofhaverstraw.us/toh_main.php?ourHistory=5&home=1&section=history&history=2|title=Town of Haverstraw: History of Haverstraw: page 5|access-date=November 7, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071018005107/http://townofhaverstraw.us/toh_main.php?ourHistory=5&home=1&section=history&history=2|archive-date=October 18, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="denoyelles_page11">de Noyelles, pp. 11–12</ref> Haverstraw has a complicated record of names. One Act refers to the Village of Waynesburgh, and will take an extract from this Act, passed April 1, 1814, again: "from thence, in a direct course as nearly as may be, to such a point in the village of Waynesburgh, late Warren, as the Commissioners, etc." For what reason the name Waynesburgh was given to the hamlet, and the length of time it remained 1883–84, have escaped search, but it is likely that the interim name was in honor of revolutionary General [[Anthony Wayne]]. Warren, the hamlet had already been called, and to Warren it was changed again. But this name was never a popular one. People had long been accustomed to blend the name of the township and village in one, and call the latter, Haverstraw. At the establishment of the present Stony Point post office in 1847, it was named North Haverstraw. Commerce was carried on, not with Warren, but Haverstraw, and the name of the village post office was Haverstraw from its organization. Influenced by these and other less important reasons, the residents of the village appealed to the Legislature for relief, and, on April 14, 1874, that body passed the following act:

"SECTION I. The name of the Village of Warren in the County of Rockland, incorporated under the provisions of the Statute of the State of New York, authorizing the incorporation of villages, is hereby changed to 'Haverstraw.' All proceedings now pending by or against the said Village of Warren shall be continued in the name of Haverstraw."<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

This village did not begin its growth as early as either [[Ramapo, New York|Ramapo]] or [[Nyack, New York|Nyack]], but for many years, until the discovery of James Wood revolutionized brick making, remained a country hamlet. In 1855, Jacob Wan-dell wrote in a letter to his sister Catherine Van Houten, the following description of the present village, at the close of the last century: "My father removed from Tappan Sloat to Haverstraw in the year 1794. There was no village there then, only one house. Captain Shepherd bought the field where the village is built, of Joseph Allison, for £10 ($25), an acre. When he moved there, it was sown with rye. The river bank was the handsomest I ever saw. From [[Grassy Point, New York|Grassy Point]] down to where James Wood first set a brick- yard, (this was on the river bank directly opposite the burying ground of the De Noyelles family), was a beautiful row of large [[chestnut]]s and [[oak]] trees, growing all along the banks. It was a beautiful walk."<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

===American Revolution (1775–1783)===
[[File:Joshua Hett Smith House from The Picturesque Hudson 1915.jpg|Treason House|thumb|200px|left]]
Strategically located on the Hudson River, the village was home to a number of skirmishes between the [[Kingdom of Great Britain|British]] Army and the [[Continental Army]] during the [[American Revolutionary War]].

The peak of [[High Tor State Park|High Tor]] Mountain on the [[Long Path]] hosted [[Continental Army]] watchfires to communicate between troops installments up and down the [[Hudson River]]. Today, watchfires are an annual [[Memorial Day]] tradition in Haverstraw. Watchfires are lit at midnight on May 30 and burn for 24 hours.

Haverstraw was the site of the most grievous treason of the early years of the United States. During the night of September 21–22, 1780, the English emissary, Major [[John André]], was rowed from the [[sloop-of-war]] ''Vulture'' to a beach below the Long Cove on the southern boundary of Haverstraw. The negotiations to sell the plans to [[West Point]] were not completed by dawn, and [[Benedict Arnold]] and André traveled to the [[Joshua Hett Smith House|Belmont House]], owned by Thomas Smith and occupied by his brother Joshua Hett Smith, on the grounds of what is now Helen Hayes Hospital in [[West Haverstraw, New York|West Haverstraw]]. The house has since been known as the Treason House.

===95th New York Volunteer Infantry===
The [[95th New York Volunteer Infantry]] fought in the [[American Civil War]] under the command of [[Ulysses S. Grant]], Major General [[James S. Wadsworth|James Samuel Wadsworth]] and [[Brigadier general (United States)|Brigadier General]] [[Edmund Rice (Medal of Honor)|Edmund Rice]].<ref name="ingmire">{{cite web|last=Ingmire|first=Lance W.|title=95th New York Infantry|url=http://95thnewyorkinfantry.com/index.html|access-date=October 28, 2010}}</ref> Company F was recruited primarily from Haverstraw.<ref>[http://dmna.state.ny.us/historic/reghist/civil/infantry/95thInf/95thInfMain.htm 95th Infantry Regiment Civil War]</ref> The infantry joined in the action of the Railroad Cut on the [[Battle of Gettysburg, First Day|first day]] of the [[Battle of Gettysburg]]. They fought many battles, including the [[Battle of Mine Run]], [[Overland Campaign|Grant's Overland Campaign]], the [[Battle of the Wilderness]], [[Battle of Spotsylvania Court House|Spotsylvania Court House]], [[Battle of North Anna|North Anna]], [[Battle of Cold Harbor|Cold Harbor]] and the [[Siege of Petersburg]]. They saw the war to the end, including engagements in the [[Battle of Globe Tavern|Battle of the Weldon Railroad]], the [[Battle of Hatcher's Run]], and the [[Appomattox Campaign]].

===Brick-making capital of the world===
Commonly referred to as "Bricktown",<ref>{{cite web |date=January 23, 2018 |url=https://www.hrmm.org/history-blog/the-pits-remembering-a-tragedy-endured-by-a-hudson-river-village |title=The Pits: Remembering a Tragedy Endured by a Hudson River Village |website=Hudson River Maritime Museum}}</ref> Haverstraw was famous for its [[brick]]-making, which was a major industry for the village. Brick-making was so popular due to the clay formed by the Hudson River's water and the rich soil that lined Haverstraw's waterfront, that it was nicknamed the "brickmaking capital of the world".<ref>{{cite news |last=Phillips |first=Lisa A. |date=February 15, 2004 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/15/nyregion/museums-chronicling-a-village-s-past-brickyard-by-brickyard.html |title=MUSEUMS; Chronicling a Village's Past, Brickyard by Brickyard |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Loftin |first=A.J. |date=August 4, 2008 |url=https://hvmag.com/archive/history-2/ |title=Haverstraw's brick industry helped build New York City |website=Hudson Valley Magazine}}</ref> Many of the old [[brownstone]] and brick structures that were constructed in New York City in the late 1890s-early 1900s were composed of bricks manufactured by Haverstraw. In the early 20th century, there were more than 40 brick-making factories lining the Hudson River within the village. Although brick-making involved all ethnic groups, 60 percent of the brickyard workers were [[African Americans]].

===Other history===
[[File:View of Front Street, Haverstraw..jpg|thumb|250px|right|Front Street from the river]]
The brick industry continued to thrive until [[World War II]], when brick began to lose its value significantly. Shortly after, the village's main industry of brickmaking declined and left the village. The economic vitality of the village greatly decreased. Because of the amount of vacancies and the relatively inexpensive housing available, the village opened up to [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic]] migration, and the village has become home to many Hispanic immigrant families since the 1950s. Many families of Hispanic descent take part in the village's annual festivals. The [[Puerto Ricans in the United States|Puerto Rican]] Day Parade and Festival take place in the village's downtown in early June, and the [[Dominican Republic|Dominican]] Day Parade and Festival occur in late August and in September.

[[File:Haverstraw Village Landslide 1906.jpg|thumb|200px|left|Great Haverstraw Landslide of 1906]] On the night of January 8, 1906, a [[landslide]] destroyed a large residential and commercial portion of the village.  Firefighters responded immediately but faced enormous odds because of burst valves and water mains, natural gas explosions and hoses which periodically froze because of the extreme cold. The landslide, a pit about {{convert|150|ft}} deep, claimed five Haverstraw blocks from Allison to Jefferson Street, 21 buildings, and the lives of 4 firefighters and 17 residents.  Despite the events, the village rebounded.  Eight years later, however, the [[Cleary-Newman murder]] took place, which cast a pall of corruption over the populace.  In 2007, leaders of the village and town announced the 101st anniversary of the landslide and dedicated a memorial to the victims of the disaster. The memorial is located at Bowline Point Park on the shore of Bowline Pond and the Hudson River.

In July 1920, [[New York Yankees]] outfielder [[Babe Ruth]] spent time in Haverstraw to film a movie – ''[[Headin' Home]]''. A local baseball field bears the Hall of Famer's name due to his visit.

[[File:View from Bowline Pond Toward High Tor.jpg|thumb|250px|Haverstraw Village from Bowline Pond]]
[[File:Two young girls at Camp Christmas Seals.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Camp buddies at Camp Christmas Seals]]

[[George M. Cohan]], the "Father of Modern Broadway", had his debut playing the violin at the Waldron's Opera House on Broadway in the village. The Cohan family stayed in Haverstraw during summer while making their rounds on the [[vaudeville]] circuit. The Cohans lived on Division Street, next to a major clay pit in the Village. Cohan was influenced early in his life by the songs of the southern black clay diggers that worked down below the Cohan house in the clay pit. It is often said that Cohan mainstreamed [[ragtime]] and [[jazz]] through his [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] tunes.

September 2004 marked the village's 150th anniversary, celebrated by a festival along the village's waterfront. The village has entered a period of revitalization, which coincides with the creation of the Harbors at Haverstraw Community and a sculpture trail which will follow the Hudson River shoreline. The Harbors at Haverstraw is situated on the southern end of the Village and below the higher elevations of the charming riverside southernmost neighborhood known as Dutchtown. Some residents have taken to calling the Harbors area the "South End" instead of the previous name for the neighborhood the "mud hole" in honor of various clay pits once visible here. The State has funded $3 million to the revitalization project, which includes investments on the waterfront [[esplanade]] and a possible downtown streetscape project.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.empire.state.ny.us/press/press_display.asp?id=222 |title=Governor: New Funds for Haverstraw Revitalization Effort |website=www.empire.state.ny.us |access-date=February 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060923015441/http://www.empire.state.ny.us/press/press_display.asp?id=222 |archive-date=September 23, 2006 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

As a cost-saving measure, at midnight on January 1, 2006, the Village of Haverstraw Police Department was merged with the Town of Haverstraw Police Department. The town of [[Clarkstown, New York|Clarkstown]] Police opened a new shooting range that the town of Haverstraw and other departments use at Tilcon Quarry area.

In April 2012, the Village of Haverstraw passed the first ban on [[Regulation of nicotine marketing|tobacco product display]] in the United States, though the New York Association of Convenience Stores and seven tobacco companies ([[Lorillard Tobacco Company]], [[R. J. Reynolds Tobacco Company]], [[Philip Morris USA]], [[Santa Fe Natural Tobacco Company]], [[American Snuff Company]], [[U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company]], and [[John Middleton Co.]]) sued to stop the ban in the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]] in June of that year.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Curry |first1=Laurel E. |last2=Schmitt |first2=Carol L. |last3=Juster |first3=Harlan |date=May 13, 2014 |title=The Haverstraw Experience: The First Tobacco Product Display Ban in the United States |journal=[[American Journal of Public Health]] |language=en |volume=104 |issue=6 |pages=e9–e12 |doi=10.2105/AJPH.2013.301861 |issn=0090-0036 |pmc=4062026 |pmid=24825238}}</ref>

===Camp Christmas Seals===
Camp Christmas Seals - (interracial camp), where children were aided by the Methodist Camp Service. Mrs. Addie C. Cox, director, the "mother" of all the campers. Activities included boating, fishing and swimming at nearby [[Lake Tiorati]], one of the seven main lakes in [[Harriman State Park (New York)|Harriman State Park]], located in [[Orange County, New York]].<ref>[https://picryl.com/search?q=%23camp%2Bchristmas%2Bseals Camp Christmas Seals]</ref>

==Geography==
[[File:Haverstraw Bay.jpg|thumb|Haverstraw Bay]]
Haverstraw is on the west bank of the [[Hudson River]]. [[Haverstraw Bay]] is the widest portion of the Hudson River. The bay is bordered by the village of Haverstraw and the village of [[Croton-on-Hudson, New York|Croton-on-Hudson]] in [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester County]] to the east.

Haverstraw is located at {{Coord|41|11|47|N|73|58|0|W|type:city}} (41.196494, −73.96684).<ref name="GR1">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/geographies/reference-files/time-series/geo/gazetteer-files.html|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=April 23, 2011|date=February 12, 2011|title=US Gazetteer files: 2010, 2000, and 1990}}</ref>

According to the [[United States Census Bureau]], the village has a total area of {{convert|13.1|sqkm|disp=flip}}, of which {{convert|5.2|sqkm|disp=flip}} is land and {{convert|8.0|sqkm|disp=flip}}, or 60.75%, is water.

==Neighborhoods==
[[File:Downtown Haverstraw NY.JPG|thumb|Downtown Haverstraw, NY]]
* Bank Corner - downtown center
* Hahn's Corner - intersection of Westside Avenue and Broadway
* South End - "the mud hole," the harbors community and surrounding residential areas
* Dutchtown - Riverside Avenue at northern terminus of the Hook Mountain Nyack Beach Trail
* Uptown - stately, residential district on Hudson Avenue and Hillside Avenue
* Little Italy - Warren Avenue and McKenzie Avenue
* Old Quarter - residential district on Front Street, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Street, bounded by Van Houten Street, Canal Street and Broad Street
* Bull Line Blaff - Jefferson Street and Clinton Street
* North Broadway - where Broadway meets Samsondale Avenue
* Silk Mill - between Gurnee Avenue and Spring Street

As of the census<ref name="GR2">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 31, 2008|title=U.S. Census website}}</ref> of 2000, there were 10,117 people, 2,816 households, and 2,168 families residing in the village. The population density was {{convert|5,078.8|PD/sqmi|PD/km2|sp=us|adj=off}}. There were 2,925 housing units at an average density of {{convert|1,468.4|/sqmi|/km2|sp=us|adj=off}}. The racial makeup of the village was 46.02% [[White (U.S. Census)|white]], 12.07% [[African American (U.S. Census)|black]] or [[Race (United States Census)|African American]], 0.37% [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 1.09% [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.13% [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 34.70% from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 5.62% from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 59.29% of the population.

There were 2,816 households, out of which 43.5% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 47.1% were married couples living together, 23.0% had a female householder with no husband present, and 23.0% were non-families. 17.9% of all households were made up of individuals, and 7.4% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 3.42 and the average family size was 3.82.

In the village, the population was spread out, with 28.6% under the age of 18, 10.9% from 18 to 24, 30.7% from 25 to 44, 18.9% from 45 to 64, and 10.9% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 32 years. For every 100 females, there were 93.0 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 89.9 males.

The median income for a household in the village was $42,683, and the median income for a family was $44,881. Males had a median income of $31,503 versus $27,207 for females. The per capita income for the village was $15,442. About 13.9% of families and 16.9% of the population were below the poverty line, including 18.4% of those under age 18 and 23.0% of those age 65 or over.

==Transportation==
[[File:New York Central Herald.svg|thumb|left|200px|NY Central RR]]
[[File:Peter R. Weiss, Haverstraw-Ossining Ferry.jpg|thumb|right|200px|''Peter R. Weiss'', Haverstraw-Ossining Ferry]]
The [[River Subdivision (CSX Transportation)|River Subdivision]] runs through the village of Haverstraw as a freight-only line, which has an important passing siding located at milepost 35. The River Subdivision is the primary freight rail line between the New York City – Northeastern [[New Jersey]] metropolitan area and [[Albany, New York|Albany]]. Today, the line is operated by [[CSX Transportation]], the fourth railroad to do so. On an average day 20–25 trains pass through Haverstraw.  Passenger service along the former [[West Shore Railroad]] line stopped on September 11, 1959,<ref>{{cite news |title=West Shore Will End All Service at Haverstraw Station Tomorrow |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/84498998/haverstraw-station-september-10-1959/ |access-date=August 31, 2021 |work=The Journal-News |date=September 10, 1959 |location=[[White Plains, New York]] |page=1|via=Newspapers.com}} {{open access}}</ref> although the former Haverstraw station building is still standing and currently serves as a law office.<ref name="stein">{{cite web|url=http://www.nycollectionlaw.com/|title=New York Collection Law, Collection Practice|access-date=November 4, 2010}}</ref>

[[NY Waterway]] runs a [[Haverstraw–Ossining Ferry|commuter ferry]] from Haverstraw Village to [[Ossining (village), New York|Ossining]], from where there are commuter trains to [[Grand Central Terminal]]. A monthly uniticket for the [[Haverstraw–Ossining Ferry]] and the train is available from [[Metro-North Railroad|Metro-North]].Local transit is operated by [[Transport of Rockland]]. The #91, #95, and #97 routes serve Haverstraw.<ref>{{Cite web |title=TOR Route Map |url=https://rocklandgov.com/files/7913/6181/9564/TOR_RouteMap.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140716190041/https://rocklandgov.com/files/7913/6181/9564/TOR_RouteMap.pdf |archive-date=2014-07-16 |website=rocklandgov.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rocklandgov.com/departments/public-transportation/transport-of-rockland/|title = County of Rockland, New York :: Transport of Rockland (TOR)}}</ref>

[[Short Line (bus company)|Short Line]], part of [[Coach USA]], provides daily service along [[U.S. Route 9W]] heading to and from the [[Port Authority Bus Terminal]] in [[Midtown Manhattan]] and [[West Point Military Academy]] or [[Newburgh (town), New York|Newburgh]].

[[U.S. Route 9W]] and [[U.S. Route 202|US 202]] run directly through the village. [[U.S. Route 9W]] is a major cycling route between [[New York City]] and [[Bear Mountain State Park]] and [[West Point Military Academy]]. The route regularly hosts the [[Gran Fondo]] cycling endurance race.

===Landmarks and places of interest===

[[File:Haverstraw King's Daughters Public Library.jpg|thumb|[[Haverstraw King's Daughters Public Library|Haverstraw King's Daughters Village Library]]]]
[[File:The Homestead, Haverstraw, NY.jpg|thumb|[[The Homestead (Haverstraw, New York)|The Homestead]]]]
[[File:Haverstraw, NY, post office.jpg|thumb|[[United States Post Office (Haverstraw, New York)|Haverstraw's U.S. Post Office]]]]
* Arts Alliance of Haverstraw, 91 Broadway, is a multicultural center for the arts.<ref name="arts_alliance">{{cite web|url=http://www.arts-alliance.org/|title=Arts Alliance of Haverstraw|access-date=November 4, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090909215102/http://www.arts-alliance.org/|archive-date=September 9, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Central Presbyterian Church, 64 New Main Street at intersection with Hudson Avenue, was founded in 1846 and moved to its present church in 1909, which was built with donated Haverstraw brick and now-scarce [[American Chestnut]] wood. The 13 stained-glass windows in the main sanctuary were designed by [[Louis Comfort Tiffany]].{{citation needed|date=January 2020}}
* House depicted in [[Edward Hopper]]'s painting ''The House By The Railroad'', located along Route 9W just north of New Main Street. The house also inspired the Bates' house set used in [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s 1960 movie ''[[Psycho (1960 film)|Psycho]]''.<ref name="wagstaff">{{Cite book| page=234| editor1-last=Wagstaff| editor1-first=Sheena| title=Edward Hopper| year=2004| publisher=Tate Publishing| location=London| isbn=1-85437-533-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Bochner |first=Paul |date=May 1996 |title=Someplace Like Home: An Eerily Familiar House Rises in Many American Landscapes |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1996/05/someplace-like-home/376584/ |journal=The Atlantic Monthly |volume=277 |issue=5 |pages=40–41 |access-date=August 24, 2014}}</ref>
* Haverstraw African American Memorial Park 41 Clinton St.  Haverstraw, NY 10927.  The park features a kiosk with displays about local history and the African diaspora.<ref>[https://www.thehaac.com/haverstraw-african-american-memoria The Haverstraw African American Connection]</ref> including the history of the African Methodist Episcopal Bethel Church, founded by slaves and free blacks in 1846. The church was Rockland's first house of worship for blacks.
**Harriet Tubman Statue - Beacon of Hope
* Haverstraw Brick Museum, 12 Main Street, has exhibits of the over 100-year history of brick-making in the Haverstraw area, once known as "the brick-making capital of the world".
* [[Haverstraw King's Daughters Public Library|Haverstraw King's Daughters Village Library]], 85 Main Street, is the oldest public library in Rockland County, chartered in 1895. The library opened in Jenkins Hall in 1896 and moved to the National Bank Building the following year. The King's Daughters Society, organized in 1891, was known as the "Haverstraw Ladies Home Mission Circle". Mrs. Everett Fowler, whose husband was president to The Peoples Bank, a state bank, presented a plan to found a public library as a department of the society.  In July 1899 the library trustees accepted Denton Fowler's proposition to match the $10,000 for the purchase of the library's present site, which included the provision that the building be named the "Fowler Library Building". The building was constructed with Haverstraw brick from the Fowlers' brickyard. The imprint DF&S can be read on the bricks laid for the basement's floor. During the holiday seasons the library provided baskets for the poor, and throughout the year the library conducted sewing classes for the girls of the village. The library was active in providing relief for the victims of the landslide in 1906. ([[National Register of Historic Places listings in Rockland County, New York|NRHP]])
* [[The Homestead (Haverstraw, New York)|The Homestead]], Hudson Avenue, is a [[historic house]] that is one of the oldest buildings in the village, dating to the early 19th century. In 1983 it was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] (NRHP).
* [[MV Commander|M/V ''Commander'']], Haverstraw Marina, is a rare design link between the heavily built-for-steam boats of the late 19th century and the more lightly built vessels of the 20th century. It was listed in 1984 on both the State and National Registers of Historic Places and is also listed in the International Register of Historic Ships, Great American Ships and the ''[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]]''.<ref name="danfs">{{cite web|url=http://www.history.navy.mil/danfs/c11/commander.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040302073821/http://history.navy.mil/danfs/c11/commander.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 2, 2004|title=Commander|publisher=[[United States Navy]]|access-date=November 4, 2010}}</ref> It may be chartered for private parties and excursions. (NRHP)
* [[United States Post Office (Haverstraw, New York)]], 86 Main Street, is listed on the NRHP.
* St. Peter's Roman Catholic Church, 115 Broadway, is the oldest [[Catholic church]] in Rockland County and is where the first [[Tridentine Mass|Mass]] was offered on November 14, 1847.
* The Congregation of the Sons of Jacob, 37 Clove Avenue, begun in 1877, is the oldest [[Judaism|Jewish]] congregation in Rockland County.

==Sports==
In 2009, Haverstraw was the Girls [[Little League Baseball]] [[Junior, Senior & Big League Baseball|Seniors Division]] state champion, beating the 2008 champion from [[New Hyde Park, New York|New Hyde Park]] by a score of 1–0, leading them to the Eastern regionals in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]].

In 2010, the team were the Girls Little League Baseball Seniors Division state and Eastern regional champions. They defeated national teams from [[Germany]], [[Puerto Rico]] and [[Guam]], before losing 3–1 to [[San Antonio]], Southwest regional champions, in the World Series Championship in [[Roxana, Delaware]], on August 14, 2010.

In 2014, Haverstraw was the Boys Junior league Baseball New York State Champions. They went on to play in the Eastern Regionals in New Jersey. In 2019 Havestraw won New York State Little League State championship and came one win away from the Little League World Series losing in the Mid-Atlantic region to Connecticut and the girls softball finished third in New York State. In 2021 the girls Little League Softball team won the New York state championship going to the Little League World Series in Greenville, NC losing in the second round to Texas and Missouri. In 2019 Havestraw Little League Softball finished third in New York. In 1958 the Havestraw Little League won New York state championship losing in the East Regionals to the eventual regional champion Connecticut.

==Notable people==
* [[Gerard Benderoth]] (February 1, 1969 - March 8, 2017), Haverstraw [[police officer|patrolman]] and [[World's Strongest Man]] competitor in 2009. Benderoth, a native of Haverstraw known as "The White Rhino", is a [[North Rockland High School]] graduate and former New York City patrolman. He turned professional in 2004 and was ranked at one time in the top 10 in the United States.
* [[George M. Cohan]] (July 3, 1878 – November 5, 1942), entertainer, playwright, composer, lyricist, actor, singer, dancer and producer.  Known as "the man who owned Broadway" in the decade before World War I, he is considered the father of American [[musical comedy]]. A full-length dramatic musical entitled ''George M'' that depicted his life and which celebrated his music was produced on Broadway in 1968, as did the [[Academy Award]]-winning film ''[[Yankee Doodle Dandy]]'' in 1942.  The Cohan family used to live on the easterly end of Division Street.
* [[Michael A. Donaldson]] (January 16, 1884 – April 12, 1970), [[United States Army]] sergeant and a recipient of the United States military's highest decoration, the [[Medal of Honor]], for his actions in France during [[World War I]].<ref name=AMOHW>{{cite web |access-date=June 17, 2009 |url=http://www.history.army.mil/html/moh/worldwari.html |title=Medal of Honor citations Archive |work=World War I War Medal of Honor Recipients |publisher=[[United States Army Center of Military History]] |date=June 8, 2009 |archive-date=October 18, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081018140904/http://www.history.army.mil/html/moh/worldwari.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* [[Derrick Lassic]] (born January 26, 1970, in the village), [[NFL]] [[running back]] and former husband of [[Arthel Neville]]
* [[Toni Morrison]], first African American to be selected for the [[Nobel Prize in Literature]], owns a home in the village. Her novel ''[[Beloved (novel)|Beloved]]'' won the 1988 [[Pulitzer Prize]] for fiction. She has earned the designation of one of the [[100 Greatest African Americans]] of the United States.
